div.p: This paper investigates how to combine fault tolerance with power management in embedded realtime systems at the same time. Fault tolerance is achieved by checkpointing, and power management is carried out via dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS). Also, we take tasks' average switched capacitances into consideration. We present a faulttolerant schedulability analysis for aperiodic tasks and derive the optimal number of checkpoints. The optimal number of checkpoints can help the task to guarantee the timing constraints and minimize the worst case execution time in the presence of faults. We then propose a scheduling scheme which carries out DVFS on the basis of the schedulability analysis for the problem of static task scheduling and voltage allocation. The problem is addressed and formulated as a linear programming (LP) problem. The simulation results show that an increase of the number of variable voltages can reduce energy consumption. Also, selecting suitable voltages for tasks can lead to drastic energy reduction even if the number of variable voltages is very small.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: With the advent and the development of embedded real-time applications, both system reliability and power management have emerged as principle design considerations in embedded real-time system designs. In the past, system reliability as well as power management has been well studied separately in embedded real-time systems. It is only recently that the trade-off between system reliability and power management has been highlighted.

Fault tolerance [1,2] is a typical policy for system reliability in embedded real-time systems. Faulttolerance computing refers to the correct execution of user programs and system software in the presence of transient faults [3]. It is typically achieved through online fault detection, checkpointing, and rollback recovery.

Power management can be achieved at various design levels. There are two main types of dynamic power management (DPM) techniques. The first includes selective shut-off or slow down of system components that are idle or underutilized [4]. The second which is often termed as dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) refers to the dynamic control of the supply voltage level for the various components in a system [5].

Recent researches [6,7,8,9] attempt to combine fault tolerance with DPM. In [6], they proposed two checkpoint placement policies with continuous voltage. But the policies can tolerant one fault only and they overlook the fact that faults may occur during checkpointing and state restoration. In [7], the researchers overcome the shortages in [6] for hard realtime systems, but the proposed methods focus on fixed-priority tasks. In [8,9], the proposed methods are too conservative. The re-execution for recovery in [8] is to execute the whole task. In [9], the speed scaling in the presence of faults is raised one by one. However, most of the literatures are concerned about periodic task set only. Furthermore, none of these researches take tasks' average switched capacitances into consideration.

In many embedded real-time systems, they have both periodic tasks and aperiodic tasks. An aperiodic task is invoked for execution at any time and may have a hard deadline or a soft deadline [10]. Aperiodic tasks can be processed with general scheduling algorithms. However, in many cases it is more efficient to process aperiodic tasks with separate algorithms which make use of the knowledge that aperiodic tasks may themselves have a variety of timing requirements.

In this paper, for given multiple discrete supply voltages and tasks with arbitrary arrival time and deadline constraints, we propose a schedulability test method. With this method, we compute the optimal number of checkpoints that a task should be inserted if possible. The optimal number of checkpoints can help the task to guarantee the timing constraints and minimize the worst case execution time in the presence of faults. Then, we use linear programming (LP) model to combine the schedulability test with DVFS technique. Under this scheme, we allocate each task with at most two discrete voltages that minimize the energy consumption.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. The related models and assumptions are presented in section 2. Section 3 provides a static checkpoint-based schedulability analysis in embedded real-time systems. Section 4 combines the schedulability analysis with DVFS technique which considers the average switched capacitance for each task. The simulation experiments and the results are presented in section 5 and section 6 concludes the paper.

div.head: Framework and Assumptions
div.p: Consider a embedded real-time system with n aperiodic tasks (or jobs), J 1 , J 2 , …, J n . Each task is modeled by a tuple J i = (A i , D i , R i , C i , k i ). The elements of the tuple are defined as follows: A i and D i are the arrival time and deadline of J i respectively (A i ≤ D i ), R i is a worst-case processor cycles required to complete J i under fault-free conditions, C i is the average switched capacitance per clock cycle for the task, and k i is the number of faults that the task should tolerate.

The system has a set V ={V 1 , V 2 , … , V m } of discrete supply voltages and a set S ={S 1 , S 2 , …, S m } of discrete clock speeds. The clock speed S i corresponds to the voltage V i . Specially, the maximal clock speed in the system is denoted as f.
In a digital CMOS circuit, the dominant source of energy consumption typically increases quadratically with the supply voltage, as indicated in [11]:
div.formula: E i = R i *C i *V i 2
div.p: (1) where R i is the worst-case processor cycles required to complete J i under fault-free conditions, C i is the average switched capacitance per clock cycle for the task, and V i is the voltage supplied to the task.

Since the supply voltage directly determines the processor's clock speed, it is often convenient to think of the energy consumption as a function of the clock speed [12]. Thus, any effective DVFS scheme should be able to vary the voltage fed to the system component and the frequency of the system clock speed [6].

In many embedded real-time systems, it has been shown that transient faults are significantly more frequent than permanent faults [13]. In the system, checkpoints are made to tolerate transient faults. The cost of a checkpoint strongly depends on the task set. Specifically, the cost required to store a checkpoint is denoted as Cs, and the cost required to retrieve a checkpoint is denoted as Cr. Both Cs and Cr are characterized by processor cycles.

We make the following assumptions related to task execution and fault arrivals: 1) tasks in J can be preempted; 2) the task set J is schedulable under faultfree conditions; 3) the checkpointing intervals for the same task are equal; 4) faults are transient and intermittent [13] and can be detected as soon as they occur in the system; and 5) the discrete voltage set V is a non-decreasing sequence.

div.head: Fault-Tolerant Schedulability Analysis
div.p: In general, we consider the case of a single task. According to the analysis in [7], the worst-case execution time WCE for a task is obtained if all k faults occur at the end of checkpoint saving. If so, the worst-case execution time can be expressed as:
div.formula: WCE(m) = R/f + mCs/f + k(Cs + Cr)/f + kR/[f(m + 1)] = [R + mCs + k(Cs + Cr) + kR/(m + 1)]/f. (2)
div.p: For simplicity, we denote R new (m) = R + mCs + k(Cs + Cr) + kR/(m + 1). The meaning of R new (m) will be discussed later in section 4. The static slack time for a task can be expressed as S = D -A -WCE(m). Our objective is to find a proper value of m for each task in the task set J to maximize the slack time which can be used by DVFS techniques to reduce system power consumption while satisfying all the timing constraints of the tasks and providing high level system reliability.

In order to address the problem, we should minimize the equation (2). We can derive the value of m which minimizes WCE by differentiating (2) with respect to m and equating the result to zero. This gives us a quadratic equation in m with one negative solution (which we ignore) and one optimal value of m, given by: m = Cs kR / -1.

The value of m should be non-negative. Also, if (3) gives a non-integral value of m, then either the floor integer or the ceiling integer of this value should be taken, according to which number would produce a less worst case execution time. We denote the value which is chosen as m* that is the optimal value for a task.

In order to get the value of m*, we define a function F as follows: F(WCE(m)) = m . So m* can be derived by the following: Example 1: For a hypothetical real-time task with parameters A = 6, D = 8, R = 80 million processor cycles, k = 2, V = {3.0v, 6.0v, 9.0v, 12.0v}, f = 120 MHz, Cs = 6 million processor cycles, and Cr = 6 million processor cycles, we get m* = 4 and S(m*) = 0.7. This implies that there is an equidistant checkpointing scheme to tolerate two faults for this task, and the worst case response time is minimized when four checkpoints are inserted. Now we change k from two to six, i.e., the system is required to tolerate up to six faults. Then, we get m* = 8 and S(m*) =-0.11. Since S(m*) < 0, no equidistant checkpointing scheme exists to tolerate up to six faults for this task.

For one thing, it increases the execution time due to the checkpoint saving cost, which is contrary to the goal of reducing the response time. So we could determine an upper bound on the number of checkpoints such that adding more checkpoints can indeed reduce the response time. □ The above analysis is concerned about the tasklevel schedulability test. On the other hand, there will be inherent correlation between tasks according to the competition among the various tasks of system resources. Therefore, we also need to consider the system-level schedulability test. Since we assume that the task set is schedulable under fault-free conditions, we only need to test the system-level schedulability in the presence of faults. In the system-level schedulability test, we focus on the maximum utilization factor of the processor.

Let FT(J i , t) denote the finished portion of the worst case execution time at the highest clock speed of the task J i at time t. The maximum utilization factor of the processor at time t is determined by the following

div.p: For simplicity, we choose special values for the time point, such as the arrival time or deadline of a task, in the schedulability test. At any time, if the utilization factor of the processor is greater than 1, the system is regarded to be un-schedulable.

Considering both aspects for embedded real-time systems, we use checkpointing to test the task-level schedulability, and use the utilization of the system to test the system-level schedulability. Based on the above analysis, we give our checkpoint-based schedulability test (CST) in Figure 1.
Procedure CST(J, f) BEGIN 1 for each J i in J, do { 1.1 calculate m* for each J i ; 1.2 solving the in-equations ( 4) and ( 6) for each J i ;

1.3 if (there is a J i of which the in-equations have no solution or there is a m* which is not contained in the solution for that J i ) return (the task set is un-schedulable); 1.4 else calculate u i for each J i ； 1.5 if (u i ≤ 1) return (the task set is schedulable); 1.6 else return (the task set is unschedulable); } END Figure 1: Checkpoint-based Schedulability Test Procedure (CST) Line 1.1 calculates the optimal value of checkpoints for each task. Line 1.2 calculates the necessary conditions (4) and ( 6). Line 1.3 checks the task-level schedulability. If the necessary conditions (4) and ( 6) are not satisfied, there will be no equidistant checkpointing scheme to guarantee the system reliability. If the optimal value of checkpoints is not in the bound of necessary conditions ( 4) and ( 6), which means that the value is either too large or too small, there will be no equidistant checkpointing scheme to satisfy the timing constraint. Line 1.4 calculates the utilization of the processor if the task can pass the task-level schedulability test. Line 1.5 checks the system-level schedulability. Line 1.6 deals with the un-schedulable cases.

As we noticed that some tasks which are destined to fail due to transient faults or timing constraints are allowed to execute. Processing of these destined-to-fail tasks is useless and wastes the limited resources. An advantage of our proposed CST is that we can detect un-schedulable tasks at early stage of execution. As a result, unfruitful processing can be eliminated.

div.head: Energy-Efficient Fault-Tolerant Scheduling Scheme
div.p: Our primary objective in this paper is that, if possible, all the timing constraints for the tasks should be ensured, even in the case of k faults occurred in a task. This requires the usage of checkpoint-based schedulability test (CST) in section 3. The secondary goal of this paper is to minimize the energy consumption of the system. This requires the usage of DVFS techniques. Specifically, we formulate the static task scheduling and discretely variable voltage allocation problem into a linear programming (LP) problem and solve it.
Before describing our voltage allocation technique, called CST-CAP, let us first clarify the meaning of notations and variables associated with each task J i in the set J:

A i: the arrival time of J i . D i : the deadline of J i (A i ＜D i ). R i : the number of processor cycles required to complete J i under fault-free conditions. C i : the average switched capacitance per clock cycle for the task. k i : the number of faults that the task J i should tolerate. m* i : the optimal number of checkpoints that the task J i should be inserted. s i (t): the processor clock speed at time t. f: the maximal processor clock speed in the system.
Cs: the cost required to store a checkpoint which is characterized by processor cycles.
Cr: the cost required to retrieval a checkpoint which is characterized by processor cycles. P i (s i (t)): the power consumed for task J i during a period of unit time starting at time t.

For a given set of n tasks J 1 , J 2 , …, J n , we sort the tasks in a non-decreasing order by their arrival times and deadlines. So we divide the time sequence into 2n-1 segments. Let t 1 , t 2 , …, t 2n denote the new ordered time sequence (Note that for some cases t i+1 = t i , 2≤i ≤2n-2).

Let x i,j,k be the total time spent with supply voltage V j for task J k during the time interval [t i , t i+1 ]. Then, the LP formulation to address the task scheduling and voltage allocation problem is:

Formula ( 9) states the constraint that every task should be executed only within the interval of its arrival time and deadline. Formula (10) ensures the constraint that the total time spent by all tasks during the time interval [t i , t i+1 ] should not exceed the time interval. Formula (11) indicates that the voltage allocation and time schedule for each task must satisfy the given total processor cycle constraint for the task in the presence of faults.

Noticed that, the right side of formula ( 11) is R new which is the minimized worst-case execution time in the presence of m* k checkpoints for a task. The checkpoint-based fault-tolerant technique increases the number of processor cycles required to complete a task and directly affects the value of optimal voltage of the task.

div.head: Simulation Experiments
div.p: Our simulation experiments were implemented in C programming language and executed on a PC with an AMD Athlon 64 processor 3000+ CPU and 512MB RAM running Windows XP. The linear programming in CST-CAP was performed using ILOG CPLEX 7.0 [14]. For simplicity, let us assume that the clock speed is linearly proportional to the supply voltage, and the energy consumption is quadratically proportional to the clock speed. Specifically, we assume that the clock speed corresponding to 12.0v is 120MHz, and the value of power function P() is normalized to P(100MHz) = 1J/second at which the average switched capacitance is 1μF. Table 1 gives an instance of a task set. The unit of execution cycles that is denoted as R i in Table 1 is million processor cycles. The cost required storing a checkpoint Cs is set to be 6 million processor cycles, and the cost required to retrieval a checkpoint Cr is set to be 6 million processor cycles.

div.head: Impact factors for CST
div.p: In this section, we would like to see the effectiveness of CST procedure as the value of fault and the checkpoint saving cost varies. The optimal value of checkpoints (m*) versus the number of faults (k) Figure 2 shows the trend of m* as different number of faults. As the number of faults increases, the optimal value of checkpoints for all tasks increases. A task that should tolerate more faults has to make more checkpoints for ensuring the system reliability. However, checkpointing potentially increases the execution time. When the number of faults increases to a certain extent, adding checkpoints can not ensure the system reliability and the timing constraint at the same time, which is unacceptable for hard real-time systems. We can also see the consistent trend according to the analysis in section 3. As we can see in section 3, m* is a monotone increasing function of k. Also, the worst case execution time WCE(m) increases with the increase of m* and k. For a certain extent, the task will certainly exceed its timing requirement. The optimal value of checkpoints (m*) versus the cost of checkpointing (Cs) Figure 3 gives the trend of m* as Cs varies. We note that as the cost of checkpointing increases, the optimal value of checkpoints decreases. Intuitively, when the cost of checkpointing becomes larger, it is better to reduce the number of checkpoints that a task should be made. Because making more checkpoints increases the probability of missing the timing constraint for the task. When the value of Cs increases to a certain extent, it is impossible to find a value of m* that can satisfy the timing constraint for a task. We can also see the consistent trend according to the analysis in section 3. As we can see in section 3, m* is a monotone decreasing function of Cs. Also, the worst case execution time WCE(m) increases with the increase of Cs. For a certain extent, the task will certainly exceed its timing requirement. Fortunately, the current study in [6,7] shows that Cs is much smaller than the number of processor cycles required to complete a task.

div.head: Experiments under CST-CAP
div.p: First, we do experiments to clarify the relation between the variety of variable voltages and the effect of energy reduction. Table 2 shows a set of processors, each of which has a number of discretely variable clock speeds, controlled by voltage. Table 3 shows the energy consumptions for the tasks with variable clock speeds. The results in Table 3 show that if the number of variable voltages is increased, energy consumption can be reduced at least. Selecting suitable voltages for tasks leads to drastic energy reduction even if the number of variable voltages is very small. For example, with Processor-2 and Processor-3, tasks have different energy consumptions. Figure 4 gives the results for the task set in Table 1 with Processor-5. 4. We use Porcessor-5 with variable average switched capacitances for tasks. The energy consumption for each grogram is shown in Table 5. The experimental results show that assigning different voltages according to the tasks' average switched capacitances can lead to drastic energy reduction. Specifically, we should assign lower voltage to the tasks whose average switched capacitances are bigger. Also, we should assign higher voltage to the tasks whose average switched capacitances are smaller.
From the results, we have the following observations:

1. An increase of the number of variable voltages may have strong impact on energy reduction. However, selecting suitable voltages for applications can also lead to drastic energy reduction even if the number of variable voltages is very small. 2. For applications whose average switched capacitance is widely varied, assigning lower voltage to the tasks whose average switched capacitances are bigger and higher voltage to the tasks whose average switched capacitances are smaller can reduce energy consumptions.

div.head: Conclusions and Future Works
div.p: In this paper, we address the problem of static task scheduling and voltage allocation with dynamically variable voltage processor. We take task's average switched capacitance into consideration and concentrate on aperiodic tasks in embedded real-time systems. Also, we combine fault tolerance with power management. Fault tolerance is achieved via checkpointing and energy is saved by dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS). Specifically, the main contributions are: (1) We propose a schedulability analysis which uses checkpoints to tolerate faults. With this method, we compute the optimal number of checkpoints that a task should be inserted if possible. The optimal number of checkpoints can help the task to guarantee the timing constraints and minimize the worst case execution time in the presence of faults. (2) We present a scheduling scheme for the problem of static task scheduling and voltage allocation and formulate the problem as a linear programming (LP) problem. The scheduling scheme combines schedulability analysis with DVFS technique. Under this scheme, we allocate each task with at most two discrete voltages that minimize the energy consumption.

Significant conclusions can be summarized from the simulation results as follows: (1) An increase of the number of variable voltages can reduce energy consumption. (2) For tasks whose average switched capacitance is widely varied, selecting suitable voltages for tasks can lead to drastic energy reduction even if the number of variable voltages is very small. Specifically, we should assign lower voltage to the tasks whose average switched capacitances are bigger. Also, we should assign higher voltage to the tasks whose average switched capacitances are smaller.

In our future work, we will consider the following aspects: (1) As this paper mainly focuses on static slack time, we would like to extend the solution to deal with dynamic cases. (2) We would like to find a method for both periodic tasks and aperiodic tasks. (3) We will consider the effects of non-uniform checkpointing intervals in a task for the task scheduling and voltage allocation problem.
